title: After My Father Died At Eighty-Six, His Second Wife Gloria Got A Letter Saying She Had Six Months To Repay His $240,000 Reverse Mortgage Or Leave The Tampa House Where She Cared For Him For Fifteen Years, Until I Read The Loan Papers At Her

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE WOMAN DAD MARRIED

My mother died of breast cancer in 2008. My father, Frank Delgado, was sixty-nine. They had been married forty-one years, and for the first year after she died, I truly thought he might die too. He stopped eating. He stopped going to his Thursday night bowling league. He sat in his recliner in the dark.
Then, in 2009, he met Gloria at a grief support group at his church in Tampa.

She was a widow too, about eight years younger than Dad, a retired school cafeteria manager with a big laugh and a lot of opinions about baseball. Within six months, Dad was eating again. Within a year, he was bowling again. In 2010, when he was seventy, they got married in the church fellowship hall with a Cuban sandwich buffet and a three-piece band.

I’m Teresa. I’m fifty-seven, an accounts manager at a hospital in Atlanta. My brother, Mike, is sixty and lives in Charlotte. We were polite to Gloria from the start. We sent her birthday cards. We spent some Christmases in Tampa.
But we were never close. If I’m honest, I kept her at arm’s length.

Some people in our family thought she married Dad for his house. My aunt said it out loud at the wedding reception. Dad’s house was a three-bedroom ranch near Bayshore Boulevard that he and Mom had bought in 1974 for $38,000. By 2010, it was worth a great deal more.
“She’s sixty-two and broke,” my aunt whispered to me over the cake. “Your father’s lonely and has a paid-off house on the bay. You do the math.”
I didn’t argue. I didn’t agree, either. I just didn’t say anything. I’ve regretted that silence for a long time.
Gloria was always kind to me. I gave her politeness in return, which is not the same thing as kindness. I didn’t understand the difference until much later.
PART 2 — FIFTEEN YEARS
For fifteen years, Gloria took wonderful care of him.

She learned to make Mom’s black beans and rice because Dad missed them. She drove him to every doctor’s appointment. When he had his first heart attack in 2014, she slept in a chair beside his hospital bed for nine nights. When his eyesight started failing, she read him the sports page every morning.

When he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2018, she became his full-time caregiver. She helped him dress. She helped him in the shower. She cut his food. She learned to manage eleven different medications.
Mike and I called every week. We visited twice a year. We sent flowers on Dad’s birthday. That was about all.
In 2017, Dad called me and told me he’d taken out a reverse mortgage on the house.

“It’s to help with Gloria’s medical bills,” he said. Gloria had had a knee replacement that year, and her insurance didn’t cover all of it. “The house is paid off. This way we can use some of what it’s worth while we’re still alive.”
I didn’t know much about reverse mortgages. I’d seen the TV commercials with the old actors. I asked him if he was sure.
“Teresa, I’m seventy-eight years old,” he said. “I’m sure.”
I let it go. I figured it was his house and his decision.
Mike was annoyed. “That’s our inheritance,” he said when I told him. “She’s spending our inheritance.”
I remember that conversation clearly. I remember thinking Mike was being petty. I also remember thinking, very quietly, that maybe our aunt had been right all along.
Dad lived nine more years after that. Gloria was beside him every single one of them.
PART 3 — THE LETTER
Dad died in January. He was eighty-six. He died at home, in the bed he’d shared with Gloria for fifteen years, with her holding his hand.
The funeral was at the same church where they met. Gloria sat in the front pew with Mike and me. She cried through the whole service. Mike sat stiffly, with his arms crossed.
Two months later, my phone rang on a Tuesday night. It was Gloria. She was sobbing so hard I couldn’t understand her at first.
“Teresa,” she finally said. “I got a letter. From the mortgage company. They say I have to leave the house.”

The letter was from the company servicing the reverse mortgage. It said that because the borrower, Frank Delgado, had died, the loan was now due and payable. The balance was about $240,000. The estate or the heirs had six months to pay off the loan or sell the house. If not, the company would begin foreclosure.
And then the sentence that broke her heart. It said that Gloria was not a borrower on the loan and had no right to remain in the property.
Gloria was seventy-four. She lived on a small pension and Social Security. She had no other home. No children of her own. No savings to speak of, after years of caring for Dad.
“Where will I go, Teresa?” she said. “I lived in this house fifteen years. Your father died in this house.”
I didn’t know what to say. I told her I’d look into it.
After I hung up, I sat in my car in my driveway for a long time. I thought about all the years I’d been polite to her. I thought about the nine nights she slept in a hospital chair.
PART 4 — MY BROTHER
“Gloria’s going to lose the house,” I said. “The reverse mortgage company says she has to leave.”
“Well,” Mike said, “that’s not our problem.”
“Teresa, think about it. If she leaves, and the house gets sold, whatever’s left after the loan comes to us. That’s what the will says. Dad left the house to us.”
That was true. Dad’s will, written before he married Gloria and never changed, left the house to Mike and me. He had left Gloria his life insurance and his car.
“She took care of him for fifteen years,” I said.
“And she got to live in a paid-off house on the bay for fifteen years,” Mike said. “Rent-free. That’s a pretty good deal.”
“Mike, she’s seventy-four. She has nowhere to go.”

“She can rent an apartment. Plenty of people do.” He sighed. “Look, I’m not trying to be cruel. But Aunt Lucy was right about her from the beginning, and you know it. Dad took out that reverse mortgage to pay her bills. Now she wants to keep living there on top of it? No.”
I hung up angry. Angry at Mike. Angry at myself, because a week earlier, I might have said the same thing.
I didn’t fully know why I was going. I think part of me wanted to prove Mike right, so I could stop feeling guilty. And part of me wanted to prove him wrong.
PART 5 — THE KITCHEN TABLE
Gloria met me at the airport. She looked smaller than I remembered. Older. She hugged me for a long time in the arrivals area.

At the house, everything was exactly as it had been when Dad was alive. His reading glasses on the side table. His bowling trophies on the shelf. Mom’s old wedding photo still on the hallway wall, right beside the photo of Dad and Gloria’s wedding. Gloria had never taken Mom’s picture down.
“Your father loved her very much,” Gloria said, when she saw me looking. “I never wanted to pretend she wasn’t here first.”
She made me café con leche and set a thick folder on the kitchen table. Her hands were shaking.
“This is everything,” she said. “All the papers from the reverse mortgage. Your father kept them in the desk. I don’t understand any of it.”
I’m an accounts manager. I read financial documents for a living. I sat down at that kitchen table and read the loan documents from beginning to end. Then I read them again.

The loan was a type called a Home Equity Conversion Mortgage, which is insured by the federal government. Dad had taken it out in 2017. Gloria was not listed as a borrower, which is why the servicer said she had no right to stay.
But on the application, under marital status, Dad had checked “married.” He had listed Gloria’s full name and her date of birth. She was sixty-six at the time.
And then, on the page where the loan officer had reviewed the household, someone had written something in the margin, in blue pen.

I read it once. Then I put my finger on it and read it again, slowly, word by word. Then I looked up at Gloria, who was watching me from across the table, terrified. > “Gloria,” I said, “I think you’re going to be all right.”
PART 6 — THE NOTE IN THE MARGIN
The handwritten note in the margin said:
